p8c: You can see the same move in a dramatized scene from the movie A Beautiful Day in the Neighborhood. Lloyd, a reporter, tells Mr. Rogers, "I can't imagine it was easy… growing up with you as a father." He doesn't collapse under that or fight it, but he does answer what's worth answering in it. He tells Lloyd that until recently his oldest son never told people about his dad, and his youngest "genuinely tested" him. Eventually the two of them found their way, and now he's very proud of both his sons. Then he says, "But you are right, Lloyd. It couldn't have been easy on them. Thank you. Thank you for that perspective." Like the two truths at bedtime, a true complaint and real love don't cancel each other out, so you can take the true part without giving up your love or defending yourself.
p9fix: Also notice what else in you answers your little one, besides what you choose to say. If their "I don't believe you" gets answered with an accusation, they can learn your love is only there as long as they take it the right way. The part of you that resents them for not believing you and the part that wants to promise them things both talk in your grown-up voice, but that doesn't make those two the same part. You might find one part doing both, two separate parts, or two blended together. Knowing which tells you whether the catch is in your love itself, or in a part that only sounds like you.
